questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with a severe headache and fever. After a thorough examination, the attending physician decides to perform a lumbar puncture to rule out meningitis. During the procedure, as the needle is advanced, it pierces several anatomical structures before entering the lumbar cistern. Which of the following structures is pierced immediately before entering the lumbar cistern?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Arachnoid mater

 

The lumbar cistern is a cerebrospinal fluid-filled space within the subarachnoid space, located below the termination of the spinal cord at approximately L1-L2. During a lumbar puncture, a needle passes through multiple anatomical layers before entering the lumbar cistern. These layers include:

 

  1. Skin
  2. Subcutaneous tissue
  3. Supraspinous ligament
  4. Interspinous ligament
  5. Ligamentum flavum
  6. Dura mater
  7. Arachnoid mater

 

The arachnoid mater is the final structure pierced before the needle enters the lumbar cistern. This layer is part of the meninges, lying directly beneath the dura mater and just above the cerebrospinal fluid within the subarachnoid space.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Ligamentum flavum: The ligamentum flavum is one of the earlier structures pierced during the lumbar puncture. It is located posterior to the dura mater and serves as a key landmark for identifying the epidural space. However, it is not the last structure pierced before entering the lumbar cistern.

 

Option C. Pia mater: The pia mater is the innermost meningeal layer that closely adheres to the surface of the spinal cord. It is not pierced during a lumbar puncture, as the procedure is designed to access the subarachnoid space without contacting the spinal cord or its associated structures.

 

Option D. Dura mater: The dura mater is the tough, outermost meningeal layer. It is pierced immediately before the arachnoid mater but is not the final structure the needle passes through before entering the lumbar cistern.

 

Educational Objective:

 

During a lumbar puncture, the arachnoid mater is the final structure pierced before the needle enters the lumbar cistern, which contains cerebrospinal fluid.

questions.stem: A patient came to the OPD with history of vision loss. On investigation optic chiasma was found compressed due to an aneurysm. Which artery is most commonly involved in such presentation?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Anterior communicating artery

 

The optic chiasma is a critical structure where fibers from the nasal retina of both eyes cross. Compression of the optic chiasma typically results in bitemporal hemianopia, a pattern of vision loss affecting the outer halves of the visual fields. One of the most common causes of optic chiasma compression is an aneurysm of the anterior communicating artery (AComA).

 

 

 

The AComA is a part of the Circle of Willis and lies in close proximity to the optic chiasma. When an aneurysm occurs in this artery, it can expand and exert pressure on the optic chiasma, leading to the characteristic vision changes.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Anterior cerebral artery: While the anterior cerebral artery is part of the Circle of Willis, its course does not directly bring it into close proximity with the optic chiasma. It is less likely to cause compression of the optic chiasma during an aneurysm.

 

Option B. Middle cerebral artery: The middle cerebral artery supplies lateral parts of the brain and is not anatomically close to the optic chiasma. It is not typically implicated in vision loss due to compression of the optic chiasma.

 

Option C. Anterior choroidal artery: The anterior choroidal artery supplies structures such as the optic tract and lateral geniculate body but does not directly compress the optic chiasma in cases of aneurysm.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Compression of the optic chiasma, leading to bitemporal hemianopia, is most commonly caused by an aneurysm of the anterior communicating artery.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man presents to the neurology clinic with sudden onset of violent, involuntary throwing movements of his right arm and leg. These movements are continuous and have significantly impaired his daily activities. His medical history is significant for hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus. Imaging studies reveal a lesion in the brain. Which of the following structures is most likely responsible for his symptoms?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Subtalamic Nucleus

 

The patient's symptoms are consistent with hemiballismus, characterized by violent, involuntary, and flinging movements of one side of the body. This condition is typically caused by a lesion in the subthalamic nucleus, part of the basal ganglia.

 

 

  • The subthalamic nucleus plays a crucial role in the indirect pathway of the basal ganglia, which inhibits excessive motor activity.
  • A lesion in the subthalamic nucleus results in reduced inhibition, leading to overactive motor circuits and the characteristic violent movements seen in hemiballismus.
  • Common causes of subthalamic nucleus lesions include ischemic stroke, often related to hypertension and diabetes mellitus, as seen in this patient.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Caudate Nucleus: The caudate nucleus is part of the basal ganglia and plays a role in motor and cognitive functions. Lesions here are more often associated with conditions such as Huntington’s disease, which leads to chorea, a smoother, "dancing-like" movement, rather than the violent flinging movements seen in hemiballismus.

 

Option B. Thalamus: The thalamus acts as a relay station for sensory and motor signals. While thalamic lesions can cause motor dysfunction, they do not specifically lead to hemiballismus.

 

Option C. Substantia Nigra: The substantia nigra is involved in dopamine production and is implicated in diseases such as Parkinson’s disease, which is characterized by bradykinesia, rigidity, and tremor, rather than the violent movements observed in this patient.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Hemiballismus is caused by a lesion in the subthalamic nucleus, resulting in violent, involuntary flinging movements on the opposite side of the body.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old woman presents to the clinic with difficulty in speech production. She is able to understand language but struggles to form coherent sentences. Neurological examination and imaging studies reveal a lesion affecting a specific area of the brain. Which of the following areas is most likely involved in her condition?
questions.solutionHtml:
;

The description of the brain regions in the explanation aligns with the role of the inferior frontal gyrus as the site of Broca's area.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Superior temporal gyrus: The superior temporal gyrus contains Wernicke’s area (Brodmann area 22), which is involved in language comprehension. Lesions in this region lead to Wernicke’s aphasia, characterized by fluent but nonsensical speech and impaired comprehension, not the symptoms seen in this patient.

 

Option C. Angular gyrus: The angular gyrus (Brodmann area 39) is involved in language processing, particularly reading and writing. Damage to this region results in symptoms such as alexia (inability to read) or agraphia (inability to write), which are not described in this case.

 

Option D. Postcentral gyrus: The postcentral gyrus (Brodmann areas 3, 1, and 2) is the primary somatosensory cortex and is involved in processing sensory input from the body. A lesion here would cause sensory deficits rather than language or speech production difficulties.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Difficulty in speech production with preserved comprehension is characteristic of Broca’s aphasia, caused by a lesion in Broca’s area, located in the inferior frontal gyrus of the dominant hemisphere.

questions.stemHtml: Identify the structure marked in the image given below:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Fornix

 

The structure marked in the image is the fornix, a major white matter tract of the brain. The fornix is part of the limbic system and plays a crucial role in transmitting signals from the hippocampus to other parts of the brain, including the mammillary bodies and the thalamus.

 

 

  • Anatomical Location: The fornix is located beneath the corpus callosum, arching over the thalamus in the midline section of the brain.
  • Function: It is primarily involved in memory consolidation and connects structures important for emotion and memory.

 

The arrow in the image points to the distinct curved structure of the fornix, confirming its identity.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Pineal gland: The pineal gland is a small endocrine gland located between the two hemispheres of the brain in a groove where the two halves of the thalamus join. It is not the structure marked in the image, as the arrow points to the fornix.

 

Option B. Falx cerebri: The falx cerebri is a dural fold that separates the two cerebral hemispheres along the midline. It is not a white matter tract and is located above the corpus callosum, making it an incorrect option.

 

Option D. Pituitary gland: The pituitary gland is located at the base of the brain, within the sella turcica of the sphenoid bone. It is part of the endocrine system and is far removed from the marked structure in the image.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The fornix is a white matter tract of the limbic system, responsible for connecting the hippocampus to other brain regions, and is located beneath the corpus callosum in a mid-sagittal view of the brain.

questions.stemHtml: A woman with right-sided loss of sensations of both the upper and lower limb complains of shooting pain from her fingers to the right shoulder and a burning sensation when touching cold water. Motor functions are normal. Which of the following structures is likely to be involved?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) B

 

The symptoms described—right-sided sensory loss affecting both the upper and lower limbs, shooting pain, and altered perception of temperature—indicate involvement of the thalamus, specifically the ventral posterior nucleus (VPN).

 

 

  • The thalamus is a major relay station for sensory information, including pain, temperature, touch, and proprioception, traveling from the body to the cerebral cortex.
  • Lesions in the thalamus can lead to thalamic pain syndrome (Dejerine-Roussy syndrome), characterized by contralateral sensory loss (e.g., right-sided loss with a left-sided lesion) and burning or shooting pain (dysaesthesia) in response to stimuli.

 

In the coronal section of the brain shown, B corresponds to the thalamus, which matches the described symptoms.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. A (Corpus Callosum): The corpus callosum connects the two cerebral hemispheres and facilitates communication between them. It does not process sensory inputs, making it an incorrect choice.

 

Option C. C (Basal Ganglia): The basal ganglia are involved in motor control, coordination, and initiation of movement. Lesions here typically lead to movement disorders (e.g., Parkinson’s or Huntington’s disease) rather than sensory deficits.

 

Option D. D (Midbrain): The midbrain houses structures like the red nucleus and substantia nigra, which are involved in motor control and coordination. It does not primarily handle sensory inputs, and motor functions were noted as normal in this patient.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Lesions in the thalamus can cause contralateral sensory deficits and dysaesthesia, including burning and shooting pain, due to its role as a sensory relay center. In this coronal brain section, the thalamus is labeled as B.

questions.stemHtml: Fibers from the marked structure end in which of the following areas of the thalamus?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Anterior nucleus

 

The structure marked in the image is the mammillary body, a part of the hypothalamus. The mammillary body is involved in the Papez circuit, which is critical for memory and emotional processing.

 

 

  • Mammillary bodies receive input from the hippocampus via the fornix.
  • From the mammillary bodies, fibers travel via the mammillothalamic tract to the anterior nucleus of the thalamus.
  • The anterior nucleus of the thalamus then relays this information to the cingulate gyrus for further processing, completing the Papez circuit.

 

Thus, fibers originating from the marked structure (mammillary body) terminate in the anterior nucleus of the thalamus.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Posterior nucleus: The posterior nucleus of the thalamus is primarily involved in sensory processing, particularly pain and temperature, and does not receive input from the mammillary bodies.

 

Option B. Reticular nucleus: The reticular nucleus is involved in regulating thalamic activity and consciousness but does not receive input from the mammillary bodies.

 

Option D. Ventral Lateral nucleus: The ventral lateral nucleus is involved in motor coordination and receives inputs from the cerebellum and basal ganglia, not the mammillary bodies.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Fibers from the mammillary body terminate in the anterior nucleus of the thalamus, a key component of the Papez circuit for memory and emotional processing.

questions.stemHtml: Identify the cranial nerve passing through the given red circled structure
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) IV

 

The red-circled structure in the image corresponds to the trochlear nerve (cranial nerve IV), which is the only cranial nerve that emerges from the dorsal aspect of the brainstem, specifically from the midbrain at the level of the inferior colliculus. The trochlear nerve is responsible for innervating the superior oblique muscle of the eye, allowing for downward and lateral movement of the eyeball.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. III (Oculomotor nerve): Incorrect. The oculomotor nerve emerges from the ventral aspect of the midbrain and passes through the superior orbital fissure. It does not pass through the circled structure.

 

Option B. V (Trigeminal nerve): Incorrect. The trigeminal nerve emerges from the pons and divides into three branches (ophthalmic, maxillary, mandibular). It does not emerge from the dorsal brainstem.

 

Option D. VI (Abducens nerve): Incorrect. The abducens nerve emerges from the pontomedullary junction and travels to the orbit to innervate the lateral rectus muscle.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The trochlear nerve (cranial nerve IV) is the only cranial nerve that emerges from the dorsal aspect of the brainstem and passes through the circled structure in the given image.

questions.stemHtml: What is the blood supply of the structure marked in the image below?

options.label: A
options.text: Anterior cerebral artery and middle cerebral artery

options.label: B
options.text: Anterior cerebral artery and posterior cerebral artery

options.label: C
options.text: Anterior cerebral artery and anterior communicating artery

options.label: D
options.text: Middle cerebral artery and posterior cerebral artery

questions.answerText: Anterior cerebral artery and anterior communicating artery
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Anterior cerebral artery and anterior communicating artery

 

The corpus callosum is primarily supplied by branches of the anterior cerebral artery (ACA), which is connected by the anterior communicating artery (AComA).

 

  • Anterior cerebral artery (ACA):
    • Supplies most of the corpus callosum, including the genu and body.
    • It also supplies medial portions of the frontal and parietal lobes.
  • Anterior communicating artery (AComA):
    • This artery connects the left and right anterior cerebral arteries and contributes to the vascular supply of the anterior portions of the corpus callosum, particularly the rostrum and genu.

 

Thus, the combination of the anterior cerebral artery and the anterior communicating artery is responsible for supplying the structure marked in the image.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Anterior cerebral artery and middle cerebral artery: The middle cerebral artery supplies lateral cortical regions and does not contribute to the corpus callosum’s blood supply.

 

Option B. Anterior cerebral artery and posterior cerebral artery: The posterior cerebral artery supplies the splenium of the corpus callosum, not the anterior portions.

 

Option D. Middle cerebral artery and posterior cerebral artery: The middle cerebral artery does not supply the corpus callosum, and this combination is incorrect.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The corpus callosum, particularly its anterior portions (rostrum and genu), is supplied by the anterior cerebral artery and the anterior communicating artery.

questions.stemHtml: Which structure is supplied by the nerve causing this elevation?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Risorius

 

The elevation in the image corresponds to the facial colliculus, which is located on the floor of the fourth ventricle in the pons. The facial colliculus is formed by the fibers of the facial nerve (cranial nerve VII) as they loop around the abducens nucleus (cranial nerve VI).

 

 

1. Facial Nerve (Cranial Nerve VII):

 

  • The facial nerve supplies the muscles of facial expression, including the risorius, which is responsible for retracting the angle of the mouth (grinning).
  • A lesion in the facial colliculus can cause paralysis of muscles supplied by the facial nerve, including the risorius, and can also affect the abducens nucleus, leading to lateral rectus palsy.

 

 

2. Sequence of Involvement:

 

  • Since the facial nerve fibers wind around the abducens nucleus, damage to the facial colliculus affects the facial nerve first (causing risorius paralysis).
  • Subsequently, it may involve the abducens nucleus, affecting the lateral rectus muscle.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Lateral rectus: The lateral rectus is supplied by the abducens nerve (cranial nerve VI), whose nucleus lies beneath the facial colliculus. While the lateral rectus can be affected secondarily in lesions of the facial colliculus, the primary involvement is of the facial nerve.

 

Option B. Superior oblique: The superior oblique is supplied by the trochlear nerve (cranial nerve IV), which is not involved in the facial colliculus.

 

Option D. Levator palpebrae superioris: The levator palpebrae superioris is supplied by the oculomotor nerve (cranial nerve III) and is not associated with the facial colliculus.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The facial colliculus is formed by the facial nerve (cranial nerve VII) looping around the abducens nucleus (cranial nerve VI). Damage to this region primarily affects the facial nerve, leading to paralysis of facial muscles, including the risorius.

questions.stemHtml: Fibres of the given structure originate from?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Hippocampus

 

The marked structure in the image is the fornix, a prominent white matter tract of the limbic system.

 

  • The fornix originates from the hippocampus, where its fibers arise.
  • It serves as a major output pathway of the hippocampus, transmitting signals to the mammillary bodies of the hypothalamus and other regions of the limbic system.

 

 

Key Features of the Fornix:

 

  1. Origin: The fibers originate from the hippocampus.
  2. Pathway: The fornix forms the posterior column, body, and anterior column, eventually ending in the mammillary body.
  3. Function: It plays a critical role in memory consolidation and emotional processing as part of the Papez circuit.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Amygdala: The amygdala is involved in emotional processing but is not the origin of the fornix.

 

Option B. Mammillary body: The mammillary body is the termination point of fornix fibers, not the origin.

 

Option C. Caudate nucleus: The caudate nucleus is a component of the basal ganglia and is not related to the fornix.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The fornix originates from the hippocampus, forming a vital connection within the limbic system and playing a crucial role in memory and emotion.

questions.stem: Which skull foramina is formed by 3 bones?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Foramen lacerum

 

The foramen lacerum is a triangular opening in the base of the skull, formed by the junction of three bones:

 

  1. Sphenoid bone
  2. Temporal bone
  3. Occipital bone

 

It is located near the junction of these bones at the base of the skull. The foramen lacerum is mostly filled with cartilage in a living person and does not transmit any significant neurovascular structures directly, although it is adjacent to important anatomical pathways like the internal carotid artery.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Foramen magnum: The foramen magnum is a large opening in the occipital bone and is not formed by three bones.

 

Option C. Foramen rotundum: The foramen rotundum is formed entirely within the sphenoid bone.

 

Option D. Foramen jugulare: The jugular foramen is formed by the temporal and occipital bones but not three bones.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The foramen lacerum is the only skull foramen formed by three bones: the sphenoid, temporal, and occipital bones.

questions.stemHtml: Which of the following marked sites does SARS-COVID 19 spread to the brain?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) A

 

The marked site A corresponds to the cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone, through which the olfactory nerve (cranial nerve I) passes.

 

  • During SARS-COVID-19 infection, the virus is known to enter the brain via the olfactory pathway.
  • The olfactory nerve fibers pass through the cribriform plate to reach the olfactory bulb, providing a direct route for the virus to spread from the nasal cavity to the central nervous system (CNS).
  • This route has been implicated in the neurological symptoms observed in COVID-19, including anosmia (loss of smell), headaches, and more severe complications such as encephalitis.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. C (Superior orbital fissure): The superior orbital fissure transmits cranial nerves related to ocular movement (III, IV, VI) and ophthalmic division of V. It is unrelated to SARS-COVID-19’s primary pathway to the brain.

 

Option C. B (Optic chiasma): While the optic chiasma lies near the sphenoid sinus, it is not the entry point for SARS-COVID-19 into the brain.

 

Option D. D (Foramen ovale): The foramen ovale transmits the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve but is not related to viral entry into the CNS.

 

Educational Objective:

 

SARS-COVID-19 spreads to the brain via the cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone at site A, utilizing the olfactory nerve pathway to enter the central nervous system.

questions.stemHtml: A patient after a road traffic accident presents to the emergency room with difficulty in swallowing and slurred speech. Investigations reveal fractures in the occipitotemporal region. Which of the following areas should be tested in order to find the nerve which is involved?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) 2

 

The patient’s symptoms of difficulty swallowing (dysphagia) and slurred speech (dysarthria) point towards involvement of the vagus nerve (cranial nerve X).

 

  • The vagus nerve supplies motor innervation to the soft palate, pharynx, and larynx, which are critical for swallowing and speech.
  • Fractures in the occipitotemporal region can impact the structures within the posterior cranial fossa, where the vagus nerve exits the skull through the jugular foramen.

 

The area marked as 2 corresponds to the soft palate and pharyngeal region, which are innervated by the vagus nerve, making this the correct choice.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. 1: This area corresponds to the frontal region, which does not involve cranial nerves associated with swallowing or speech.

 

Option C. 3: This area represents the tongue, which is primarily innervated by the hypoglossal nerve (cranial nerve XII). While the hypoglossal nerve is responsible for tongue movement, it is not the primary nerve involved in swallowing and speech coordination.

 

Option D. 4: This area corresponds to the larynx, which is also innervated by the vagus nerve but does not primarily explain swallowing difficulties and palate involvement.

 

Educational Objective:

 

In cases of swallowing and speech difficulty caused by occipitotemporal fractures, the vagus nerve (cranial nerve X) is most likely involved. Testing the soft palate and pharyngeal region (marked as 2) is critical for confirming the involvement.

questions.stemHtml: At which level does the nerve supply for the marked muscle arise?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Red nucleus

 

The marked muscle in the image is the medial rectus, which is responsible for adduction of the eyeball (moving it inward). The medial rectus is supplied by the third cranial nerve (oculomotor nerve). The nucleus of the third cranial nerve is located at the level of the superior colliculus of the midbrain, where the red nucleus is also present.

 

The red nucleus is a distinctive, iron-containing structure found at this level in the midbrain and serves as a key anatomical landmark.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Subthalamic nuclei: The subthalamic nucleus is part of the basal ganglia and is involved in motor control, not in the cranial nerve supply to muscles. It is located in the diencephalon and does not relate to the medial rectus or its nerve supply.

 

Option C. Decussation of pyramidal tract: The decussation of the pyramidal tract occurs at the junction of the medulla and spinal cord, primarily involving the crossing over of motor fibers. It has no connection to the third cranial nerve or the medial rectus.

 

Option D. Olivary nucleus: The olivary nucleus is a structure in the medulla involved in motor learning and coordination. It does not play a role in the innervation of the medial rectus muscle.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The medial rectus muscle is supplied by the third cranial nerve, whose nucleus is located at the level of the superior colliculus in the midbrain, near the red nucleus.

questions.stemHtml: During climbing the staircase, a person suddenly fell & a sharp object hit on his neck. After the injury, the patient is unable to shrug/ elevate the shoulder & he is having difficulty in turning his head. What structure is most likely to be damaged?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Spinal Accessory nerve

 

The spinal accessory nerve (cranial nerve XI) is primarily responsible for innervating the trapezius and sternocleidomastoid muscles. Damage to this nerve typically results in:

 

  • Inability to shrug or elevate the shoulder due to loss of trapezius function.
  • Difficulty turning the head to the opposite side, as the sternocleidomastoid assists in head rotation.

 

In this case, the sharp object likely injured the spinal accessory nerve, causing these characteristic deficits.

 

The trapezius muscle, which is innervated by the spinal accessory nerve, has an upper fiber responsible for scapular elevation. The inability to shrug is a hallmark sign of trapezius dysfunction. Similarly, the sternocleidomastoid aids in head rotation and neck flexion, further implicating the spinal accessory nerve when its function is impaired.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Long thoracic nerve: The long thoracic nerve innervates the serratus anterior muscle, which is responsible for protracting and stabilizing the scapula. Damage to this nerve results in a "winged scapula," not difficulty in shrugging the shoulder or turning the head.

 

Option C. Sternocleidomastoid: While the sternocleidomastoid is involved in turning the head, it is not directly implicated as the primary structure in this injury. Instead, its dysfunction is due to spinal accessory nerve damage, which supplies it.

 

Option D. Deltoid: The deltoid muscle is innervated by the axillary nerve and is responsible for shoulder abduction. Damage to the deltoid or its nerve supply would not result in difficulty shrugging the shoulder or head rotation.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The spinal accessory nerve (cranial nerve XI) innervates the trapezius and sternocleidomastoid muscles. Injury to this nerve leads to an inability to shrug the shoulder and difficulty turning the head.

questions.stem: A patient presented with swelling below the ear & complained of pain in the lobule of the ear. He is having difficulty in eating food. What nerve is most likely to be damaged?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Greater Auricular nerve

 

The greater auricular nerve supplies the skin over the parotid gland, the angle of the mandible, and the lobule of the ear. Pain and swelling in these areas are characteristic of irritation or damage to this nerve, often associated with conditions affecting the parotid region, such as infections, trauma, or surgical complications.

 

In this patient, the swelling below the ear and pain in the lobule strongly suggest involvement of the greater auricular nerve, as it innervates these regions. The patient’s difficulty eating may be due to associated pain or discomfort from swelling in the parotid region.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Auriculotemporal nerve: The auriculotemporal nerve is a branch of the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve. It provides sensory innervation to the anterior part of the external ear and the temporal region. While it is involved in conditions like Frey's syndrome and parotid gland-related issues, it does not typically cause pain localized to the ear lobule or swelling below the ear.

 

Option C. Facial nerve: The facial nerve primarily provides motor innervation to the muscles of facial expression and does not supply sensory fibers to the lobule of the ear. Damage to the facial nerve would result in motor deficits such as facial weakness or paralysis, which are not present in this case.

 

Option D. Vagus/Inferior alveolar nerve: The vagus nerve and the inferior alveolar nerve are unrelated to the sensory innervation of the lobule of the ear. The vagus nerve is primarily involved in autonomic functions and some sensory innervation of the external ear, but not the lobule specifically. The inferior alveolar nerve is involved in the innervation of the teeth and chin, not the ear.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The greater auricular nerve is the primary sensory nerve supplying the skin over the parotid gland, the angle of the mandible, and the ear lobule. Damage or irritation to this nerve causes pain and swelling in these regions.

questions.stem: A man suffered an injury on head and after this the blood collected around the eyes. Which of the following layer is responsible for this condition?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Loose areolar layer

 

The loose areolar tissue layer is the fourth layer of the scalp, lying between the aponeurotic layer and the periosteum. This layer is often referred to as the "dangerous area of the scalp" because it is loosely attached and provides a potential space for blood or infections to spread.

 

In the case of a head injury, blood can collect in the loose areolar layer. This layer does not have any bony attachment on the anterior side, allowing blood to track anteriorly and accumulate around the eyes, causing the characteristic discoloration referred to as a "black eye," "panda sign," or "raccoon eye."

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Periosteum: The periosteum (or pericranium) is the innermost layer of the scalp and is closely adhered to the skull. While it plays a role in head injuries, it does not allow for blood to spread anteriorly to the eyes because it is tightly bound to the bone, limiting its role in such conditions.

 

Option B. Aponeurotic layer: The aponeurotic layer (galea aponeurotica) is the third layer of the scalp, connecting the frontalis and occipitalis muscles. It is not involved in allowing blood to spread to the eyes after an injury because it is firmly attached to surrounding tissues.

 

Option D. Connective tissue layer: The connective tissue layer is the second layer of the scalp, which is dense and contains blood vessels and nerves. While it is involved in scalp injuries, it does not have the anatomical characteristics required for blood to collect around the eyes.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The loose areolar layer of the scalp is responsible for the spread of blood to the periorbital region following head injuries, resulting in a "black eye" or "raccoon eye." This layer's loose attachment and lack of anterior bony attachment make it a key site for blood accumulation.

Educational Objective: The loose areolar layer of the scalp is responsible for the spread of blood to the periorbital region following head injuries, resulting in a "black eye" or "raccoon eye." This layer's loose attachment and lack of anterior bony attachment make it a key site for blood accumulation.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old male patient presents to the clinic with a concern about a "visible vein" in his right shoulder area. He reports that the vein becomes more pronounced during exercise or when lifting heavy objects. There is no associated pain, redness, or swelling. He denies any history of trauma to the area. On inspection of the right shoulder area reveals a prominent, non-pulsatile, linear structure running along the deltopectoral groove is seen. Which of the following structure is seen in this area
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Cephalic vein

 

The cephalic vein is a superficial vein located in the upper limb that travels through the deltopectoral groove, the space between the deltoid and pectoralis major muscles. This groove lies just below the clavicle and is covered by the clavipectoral fascia.

 

The cephalic vein is visible and may become more pronounced during activities like exercise or lifting due to increased blood flow and venous engorgement. In this patient, the absence of pain, redness, swelling, or trauma further supports that this prominent vein is the cephalic vein rather than a pathological finding.

 

The clavipectoral fascia is a fibrous layer extending between the clavicle and pectoralis minor. It is pierced by several structures, including the cephalic vein, thoracoacromial artery, lateral pectoral nerve, and lymphatics. These anatomical features help identify the vein as the cephalic vein.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Axillary artery: The axillary artery is located deep in the axilla (armpit) and does not traverse the deltopectoral groove. Additionally, the axillary artery is a pulsatile structure, unlike the vein described in this case.

 

Option C. Basilic vein: The basilic vein is another superficial vein of the upper limb, but it is located on the medial side of the arm. It does not run along the deltopectoral groove and is not visible in this region.

 

Option D. Radial nerve: The radial nerve is a major nerve of the upper limb, responsible for innervating the extensor muscles and providing sensation to parts of the hand. It does not pass through the deltopectoral groove and is not visible superficially.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The cephalic vein is a prominent superficial vein that runs along the deltopectoral groove and can become more visible during exercise or heavy lifting due to increased venous return.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT true about the trochlear nerve?

options.label: B
options.text: Supplies the ipsilateral superior oblique muscle

options.label: C
options.text: Only cranial nerve that arises from the dorsal aspect of the brainstem

options.label: D
options.text: Enters orbit through the superior orbital fissure outside the annulus of zinn

questions.answerText: Supplies the ipsilateral superior oblique muscle
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Supplies the ipsilateral superior oblique muscle

 

The trochlear nerve (cranial nerve IV) has unique features among the cranial nerves. It is responsible for innervating the superior oblique muscle, which controls eye movements, particularly depression and intorsion when the eye is adducted. However, the trochlear nerve crosses to the opposite side before innervating the superior oblique. Thus, the right superior oblique muscle is supplied by the left trochlear nerve, and the left superior oblique muscle is supplied by the right trochlear nerve. It does not supply the ipsilateral superior oblique muscle.

 

Key Features of the Trochlear Nerve:

 

  1. Longest Intracranial Course: It travels the longest intracranial distance among cranial nerves.
  2. Dorsal Origin: It is the only cranial nerve that arises from the dorsal aspect of the brainstem (midbrain).
  3. Pathway to the Orbit: It enters the orbit through the superior orbital fissure, passing outside the annulus of Zinn.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Has the longest intracranial course: True. The trochlear nerve travels a long path within the cranial cavity before reaching the orbit.

 

Option C. Only cranial nerve that arises from the dorsal aspect of the brainstem: True. The trochlear nerve originates from the dorsal side of the midbrain, a unique feature among cranial nerves.

 

Option D. Enters orbit through the superior orbital fissure outside the annulus of Zinn: True. The trochlear nerve passes through the superior orbital fissure but remains outside the common tendinous ring (annulus of Zinn).

 

Educational Objective:

 

The trochlear nerve (cranial nerve IV) is the only cranial nerve to arise from the dorsal brainstem and decussate to supply the contralateral superior oblique muscle. It has the longest intracranial course and enters the orbit outside the annulus of Zinn.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old male presents with anterior knee pain that worsens with activities like running and jumping. On physical examination, there is tenderness and swelling over the front of the knee. Palpation reveals a small, round, bony prominence at the centre of the knee. The patient reports no recent trauma. You will put the involved bone in which of the following type
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Sesamoid

 

The bony prominence described in the question is the patella, which is a sesamoid bone. Sesamoid bones are small, rounded bones embedded within tendons, usually located near joints. The patella is the largest sesamoid bone in the human body, situated in the quadriceps tendon over the knee joint. It functions to protect the knee joint and improve the leverage of the quadriceps muscle during movement.

 

In this patient, the pain and swelling over the front of the knee, along with the history of activities like running and jumping, point toward patellar tendinopathy or overuse injury. The patella’s structure and function classify it as a sesamoid bone.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Sphenoid: The sphenoid bone is an unpaired cranial bone located at the base of the skull. It has no relevance to the knee or its anatomy.

 

Option B. Hyoid: The hyoid bone is a U-shaped bone in the neck, supporting the tongue and associated with swallowing. It is not related to the knee joint.

 

Option C. Ethmoid: The ethmoid bone is a cranial bone located between the eyes, contributing to the nasal cavity and the orbits. It is not related to the patella or knee anatomy.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The patella is the largest sesamoid bone in the human body. Sesamoid bones are found within tendons near joints and serve to protect the joint and enhance muscle function.

questions.stem: Where is the growth plate of cartilage in a long bone located?

options.label: B
options.text: Between the diaphysis and the epiphysis

questions.answerText: Between the diaphysis and the epiphysis
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Between the diaphysis and the epiphysis

 

The growth plate, also known as the epiphyseal plate, is a layer of hyaline cartilage found in growing bones. It is located between the diaphysis (shaft) and the epiphysis (ends of the bone). This plate is responsible for longitudinal growth in long bones during childhood and adolescence.

 

 

The cartilage in the epiphyseal plate undergoes a process of endochondral ossification, where cartilage is replaced by bone tissue as the bone grows in length. Once the bone reaches its mature length, the epiphyseal plate is replaced with bone, forming the epiphyseal line.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. In the diaphysis: The diaphysis is the shaft of the long bone and does not contain the growth plate. It is primarily composed of compact bone and houses the medullary canal.

 

Option C. In the epiphysis: The epiphysis is the rounded end of the long bone and contains spongy bone and red marrow. While it is adjacent to the growth plate, the growth plate itself is not located within the epiphysis.

 

Option D. In the medullary canal: The medullary canal is the hollow, central part of the diaphysis, primarily containing bone marrow and not involved in bone growth.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The epiphyseal plate (growth plate) is located between the diaphysis and the epiphysis and is responsible for the longitudinal growth of long bones through endochondral ossification.

questions.stemHtml: A 21 years old patient Suyash came to OPD with history of fall on hand. Now he is having pain at hand region. X ray of patient is given. Which of the following joint has been shown in his X ray ?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Ellipsoid joint.

 

The X-ray shows the wrist joint (radiocarpal joint), which is an ellipsoid joint. This type of synovial joint permits movements such as flexion, extension, abduction, and adduction but restricts rotation.

 

The wrist joint involves articulation between the distal radius and the carpal bones (primarily the scaphoid and lunate). This joint's structure and function classify it as an ellipsoid joint.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Hinge joint: Hinge joints allow uniaxial movement, such as flexion and extension, seen in joints like the elbow or knee. This does not apply to the wrist joint.

 

Option B. Ball-and-socket joint: Ball-and-socket joints allow multiaxial movements, such as in the shoulder and hip. The wrist joint does not fall into this category as it lacks a ball-like structure and full rotational movement.

 

Option D. Saddle joint: Saddle joints permit biaxial movement and are found in the thumb's carpometacarpal joint. This is not the case for the wrist joint.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The wrist joint (radiocarpal joint) is an ellipsoid joint that allows movements such as flexion, extension, abduction, and adduction but limits rotation.

questions.stem: What is the typical fiber arrangement of lumbrical muscles in the hand?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) 1st & 2nd lumbricals – Unipennate, 3rd & 4th lumbricals – bipennate

 

The lumbrical muscles of the hand are four small intrinsic muscles that originate from the tendons of the flexor digitorum profundus. Their fiber arrangement differs as follows:

 

  • 1st and 2nd lumbricals: These are unipennate muscles, meaning their fibers are arranged on one side of the tendon.
  • 3rd and 4th lumbricals: These are bipennate muscles, meaning their fibers are arranged on both sides of the tendon.

 

This arrangement corresponds to the orientation and function of these muscles in controlling fine movements of the fingers.

 

Key Roles of the Lumbricals:

 

  • Flexion at the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints.
  • Extension at the interphalangeal (IP) joints.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The lumbricals of the hand have the following fiber arrangement:

 

  • 1st and 2nd lumbricals: Unipennate.
  • 3rd and 4th lumbricals: Bipennate.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman presents to the emergency department after falling onto her outstretched hand. She complains of severe pain in her elbow. Physical examination reveals swelling and tenderness over the distal humerus. An X-ray confirms a supracondylar fracture. Upon further examination, the patient is unable to flex her thumb. Which nerve is most likely involved in this patient's presentation?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Anterior interosseous nerve

 

The anterior interosseous nerve is a branch of the median nerve. It arises in the forearm and innervates the deep flexor muscles of the forearm, including:

 

  • Flexor pollicis longus (FPL) – responsible for flexing the thumb.
  • Pronator quadratus – responsible for pronation of the forearm.
  • The lateral half of the flexor digitorum profundus (FDP) – responsible for flexing the distal interphalangeal joints of the index and middle fingers.

 

In this patient with a supracondylar fracture, the anterior interosseous nerve is likely injured, resulting in the inability to flex the thumb. This type of injury can occur due to the proximity of the median nerve to the distal humerus.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Deep branch of ulnar nerve: The deep branch of the ulnar nerve innervates intrinsic hand muscles, including the interossei and lumbricals, and is unrelated to thumb flexion.

 

Option B. Posterior interosseous nerve: The posterior interosseous nerve, a branch of the radial nerve, innervates the extensor muscles of the forearm. It is involved in extension, not flexion, of the thumb.

 

Option D. Superficial branch of ulnar nerve: The superficial branch of the ulnar nerve is responsible for sensory innervation to the medial aspect of the hand and does not affect thumb flexion.

 

Educational Objective:

 

In a supracondylar fracture of the humerus, injury to the anterior interosseous nerve (branch of the median nerve) can result in an inability to flex the thumb due to its innervation of the flexor pollicis longus. This highlights the importance of the median nerve's role in thumb flexion.

questions.stem: A surgeon is performing a dissection in the shoulder region and notes the structures passing through the clavipectoral fascia. Which of the following structures is known to pierce the clavipectoral fascia?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Thoracoacromial Artery

 

The clavipectoral fascia is a fibrous sheet located in the shoulder region, between the clavicle and the pectoralis minor muscle. Several structures pierce the clavipectoral fascia as they pass through it, which can be remembered using the mnemonic "TALC":

 

  • T: Thoracoacromial artery
  • A: Accompanying lymphatics
  • L: Lateral pectoral nerve
  • C: Cephalic vein

 

The thoracoacromial artery, a branch of the axillary artery, is one of the key structures piercing this fascia, supplying the pectoral and deltoid regions.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Axillary Nerve: The axillary nerve does not pierce the clavipectoral fascia. It passes through the quadrangular space along with the posterior circumflex humeral artery to supply the deltoid and teres minor muscles.

 

Option C. Suprascapular Artery: The suprascapular artery travels over the scapula, supplying the supraspinatus and infraspinatus muscles, and does not pierce the clavipectoral fascia.

 

Option D. Long Thoracic Nerve: The long thoracic nerve runs along the lateral thoracic wall to supply the serratus anterior muscle but does not pierce the clavipectoral fascia.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The thoracoacromial artery is one of the key structures piercing the clavipectoral fascia, along with the cephalic vein, lateral pectoral nerve, and lymphatics. This anatomical relationship is essential for understanding the vascular and nervous supply in the shoulder region.

questions.stemHtml: A 60-year-old patient presents to the orthopedic clinic with complaints of progressive weakness in his right hand. The patient reports difficulty in fine movements of hand. Doctor performed a test over patient as shown in image. Which of the following statements is true about the given image?

options.label: A
options.text: The median nerve of the right hand is injured.

options.label: B
options.text: There is weakness of thenar muscles on the right side

options.label: C
options.text: The adductor pollicis of the right side is weak

options.label: D
options.text: The flexor muscles of the thumb of the right hand is weak

questions.answerText: The adductor pollicis of the right side is weak
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) The adductor pollicis of the right side is weak

 

The test shown in the image is called the Froment’s sign, commonly used to assess ulnar nerve dysfunction. In this test, the patient is asked to hold an object, such as a sheet of paper, between their thumb and index finger (pinch grip). The adductor pollicis, which is responsible for thumb adduction, is supplied by the ulnar nerve.

 

When the ulnar nerve is damaged, the patient compensates for the weak adductor pollicis by flexing the thumb using the flexor pollicis longus, which is supplied by the median nerve. This results in the thumb assuming a flexed position, as seen in the image.

 

Key Findings in the Image:

 

  1. The normal hand (left) holds the paper using thumb adduction (straight thumb axis).
  2. The affected hand (right) shows thumb flexion, indicating adductor pollicis weakness.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. The median nerve of the right hand is injured: Incorrect. The test indicates a compensatory use of the flexor pollicis longus (supplied by the median nerve) due to ulnar nerve injury, not median nerve dysfunction.

 

Option B. There is weakness of thenar muscles on the right side: Incorrect. The thenar muscles are supplied by the median nerve, but this test primarily evaluates the function of the adductor pollicis, which is innervated by the ulnar nerve.

 

Option D. The flexor muscles of the thumb of the right hand are weak: Incorrect. The flexor muscles (flexor pollicis longus and brevis) are functional in this case and are compensating for the weak adductor pollicis.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The Froment’s sign is a clinical test for ulnar nerve dysfunction, specifically testing the function of the adductor pollicis. Weakness of the adductor pollicis results in compensatory flexion of the thumb, which is supplied by the median nerve.

questions.stemHtml: A 17-year-old, who was going to represent his college football team in an intercollege sports event, after one of his practice sessions felt a vague pain over the inner side of his midfoot just above the longitudinal arch. His orthopedician also noted redness, tenderness and swelling in the area pointed out by the patient. The below image is the X-ray of the patient’s foot. Which of the following statements is true pertaining to the arrow pointed in the above image?

options.label: B
options.text: There is fracture of navicular bone

options.label: C
options.text: This bone is participating in lateral longitudinal arch

options.label: D
options.text: Supination & pronation occurs at this joint

questions.answerText: There is fracture of navicular bone
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) There is fracture of navicular bone

 

The image indicates a fracture of the navicular bone, a boat-shaped bone located on the medial side of the midfoot. The navicular bone forms an essential component of the medial longitudinal arch and is critical for weight-bearing and stabilization of the foot.

 

  • Fracture Identification: The pain, swelling, and tenderness over the midfoot, along with the X-ray findings, strongly suggest a navicular bone fracture, commonly seen in athletes due to repetitive stress or trauma.
  • Anatomical Position: The navicular bone lies anterior to the talus and articulates with the cuneiform bones and the talus, making it a critical part of the medial longitudinal arch.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. This is a sesamoid bone: Incorrect. The navicular bone is not a sesamoid bone. Sesamoid bones are embedded within tendons and are typically found in locations such as the thumb (in the hand) and the great toe (in the foot).

 

Option C. This bone is participating in the lateral longitudinal arch: Incorrect. The navicular bone is part of the medial longitudinal arch, not the lateral longitudinal arch, which consists of the calcaneus, cuboid, and lateral metatarsals.

 

Option D. Supination and pronation occur at this joint: Incorrect. Supination and pronation primarily occur at the subtalar joint, not at the navicular bone. The subtalar joint is located between the talus and calcaneus.

 

Educational Objective:

 

A navicular bone fracture is a common injury in athletes, especially due to repetitive stress or acute trauma. It plays a key role in the medial longitudinal arch of the foot and requires careful clinical and radiological assessment for diagnosis
