questions.stemHtml: A 22-year-old male athlete sustained an injury to his foot during one of his practice sessions. The given image is the x-ray of his foot. Which of the following statements is true pertaining to the given image?

options.label: A
options.text: It is fracture of first metatarsal base

options.label: B
options.text: It is a fracture of fifth metatarsal base

options.label: C
options.text: The tuberosity of the pointed bone in the above image is least vascular

options.label: D
options.text: Its metadiaphyseal region receives the insertion of peroneus tertius tendon

questions.answerText: It is a fracture of fifth metatarsal base
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) It is a fracture of fifth metatarsal base

 

The X-ray shows a fracture of the base of the fifth metatarsal, commonly known as a Jones fracture. This type of fracture occurs in the proximal portion of the fifth metatarsal and is typically caused by a sudden twisting motion of the foot or excessive stress, such as during sports or athletic activities.

 

Key Features:

 

  • The fifth metatarsal base is a common site of fracture due to its anatomical location and stress from the tendons attaching to it.
  • The peroneus brevis muscle inserts at the tuberosity of the fifth metatarsal. Forceful contraction of this muscle can cause avulsion fractures in this region.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. It is a fracture of the first metatarsal base: Incorrect. The fracture clearly involves the base of the fifth metatarsal, not the first.

 

Option C. The tuberosity of the pointed bone in the above image is least vascular: Incorrect. The tuberosity of the fifth metatarsal is relatively vascular. However, the metadiaphyseal region of the fifth metatarsal, which is more distal, has poor vascularity, leading to delayed healing in Jones fractures.

 

Option D. Its metadiaphyseal region receives the insertion of peroneus tertius tendon: Incorrect. The peroneus brevis tendon inserts at the tuberosity of the fifth metatarsal, while the peroneus tertius inserts more distally on the shaft of the fifth metatarsal.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The fifth metatarsal base is commonly fractured in athletic injuries, often caused by the pull of the peroneus brevis tendon. This type of fracture is important to differentiate from other midfoot injuries due to its implications for healing and treatment.

questions.stem: An 18-year-old female while driving her two wheeler accidentally collided with a car from the opposite side on her way to college. She failed to balance her vehicle and eventually fell down while the vehicle dropped over her left lower leg. X-ray revealed fracture of lower fibula and cast was applied. Few days after this, she developed pain and numbness over most of the dorsum of her left foot and had difficulty in turning her sole outwards. Which could be the most probable sight of nerve compression in this patient?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Lateral compartment of leg

 

The patient is having the difficulty of turning the sole outward. I.e., she is having difficulty in extortion which is produced by the muscles of the latera;l compartment of the leg.

 

The lateral compartment of the leg houses two key muscles:

 

  • Peroneus longus
  • Peroneus brevis

 

These muscles are responsible for eversion of the foot. Both are innervated by the superficial peroneal nerve. A fracture of the fibula can compress or damage this nerve, leading to:

 

  1. Pain and numbness over the dorsum of the foot (except the first web space, which is innervated by the deep peroneal nerve).
  2. Weakness or inability to evert the foot, as seen in this case.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Dorsum of foot: The dorsum of the foot shows sensory changes due to the involvement of the superficial peroneal nerve, but the site of compression is not located here.

 

Option C. Anterior compartment of leg: The anterior compartment contains muscles responsible for dorsiflexion and is innervated by the deep peroneal nerve, not the superficial peroneal nerve. The symptoms in this case (e.g., eversion difficulty) are related to lateral compartment involvement.

 

Option D. Posterior compartment of leg: The posterior compartment contains muscles responsible for plantarflexion and inversion, innervated by the tibial nerve. This compartment is unrelated to the patient's symptoms.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The superficial peroneal nerve, located in the lateral compartment of the leg, is responsible for eversion of the foot and sensory innervation of most of the dorsum of the foot. Fractures of the fibula may lead to nerve compression in this compartment, resulting in pain, sensory changes, and difficulty with eversion.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old male presents with a painful swelling in his right groin area. On physical examination, a bulge is noted at the mid inguinal point, which is located midway between the anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic symphysis. This finding is most suggestive of which of the following conditions?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Indirect Inguinal Hernia

 

The mid-inguinal point is located halfway between the anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS) and the pubic symphysis. It marks the location of the deep inguinal ring, which is the starting point of an indirect inguinal hernia.

 

 

 

In indirect inguinal hernia, abdominal contents (usually loops of intestine) protrude through the deep inguinal ring into the inguinal canal and may extend to the scrotum. It is the most common type of hernia and typically occurs in younger individuals due to a patent processus vaginalis.

 

Key differentiating features of an indirect inguinal hernia:

 

  1. Location: Starts at the deep inguinal ring (mid-inguinal point).
  2. Course: Travels through the inguinal canal and exits through the superficial inguinal ring.
  3. Prominence: Bulge at the mid-inguinal point, especially during coughing or straining.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Femoral Hernia: Incorrect. A femoral hernia presents as a bulge below the inguinal ligament, often near the femoral canal. It is more common in women and does not involve the mid-inguinal point.

 

Option C. Direct Inguinal Hernia: Incorrect. A direct inguinal hernia occurs due to weakness in the abdominal wall at Hesselbach’s triangle, medial to the inferior epigastric vessels. The bulge is usually closer to the superficial inguinal ring, not the mid-inguinal point.

 

Option D. Spigelian Hernia: Incorrect. A Spigelian hernia is a rare hernia that occurs along the semilunar line, lateral to the rectus abdominis muscle. It does not present as a bulge in the groin area.

 

Educational Objective:

 

A bulge at the mid-inguinal point is a hallmark of an indirect inguinal hernia, as this corresponds to the location of the deep inguinal ring, the entry point for this type of hernia.

questions.stem: A fourth-year medical student is revising the anatomy of the lower limb and focuses on the compartments of the thigh and their nerve supply. Which of the following correctly matches the three main compartments of the thigh with their respective innervating nerves?

options.label: A
options.text: Anterior compartment: Femoral nerve; Medial compartment: Sciatic nerve; Posterior compartment: Obturator nerve

options.label: B
options.text: Anterior compartment: Sciatic nerve; Medial compartment: Femoral nerve; Posterior compartment: Obturator nerve

options.label: C
options.text: Anterior compartment: Femoral nerve; Medial compartment: Obturator nerve; Posterior compartment: Sciatic nerve

options.label: D
options.text: Anterior compartment: Obturator nerve; Medial compartment: Sciatic nerve; Posterior compartment: Femoral nerve

questions.answerText: Anterior compartment: Femoral nerve; Medial compartment: Obturator nerve; Posterior compartment: Sciatic nerve
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Anterior compartment: Femoral nerve; Medial compartment: Obturator nerve; Posterior compartment: Sciatic nerve

 

The thigh is divided into three compartments, each with distinct functions, muscle groups, and nerve supply:

 

  1. Anterior Compartment:
    • Function: Knee extension and hip flexion.
    • Muscles: Quadriceps femoris group (rectus femoris, vastus medialis, vastus lateralis, vastus intermedius), sartorius, iliopsoas.
    • Nerve Supply: Femoral nerve (L2–L4).
  2. Medial Compartment:
    • Function: Hip adduction.
    • Muscles: Adductor longus, adductor brevis, adductor magnus (adductor part), gracilis, obturator externus.
    • Nerve Supply: Obturator nerve (L2–L4).
  3. Posterior Compartment:
    • Function: Knee flexion and hip extension.
    • Muscles: Hamstrings (biceps femoris, semitendinosus, semimembranosus).
    • Nerve Supply: Sciatic nerve (tibial and common peroneal branches).

 

Educational Objective:

 

The nerve supply of the compartments of the thigh is as follows:

 

  • Anterior compartment: Femoral nerve.
  • Medial compartment: Obturator nerve.
  • Posterior compartment: Sciatic nerve.

questions.stem: During a practical session in anatomy, a group of medical students are asked to identify the nerve supply to the three compartments of the leg. Which of the following correctly associates each compartment of the leg with its respective innervating nerve?

options.label: A
options.text: Anterior compartment: Superficial peroneal nerve; Lateral compartment: Deep peroneal nerve; Posterior compartment: Tibial nerve

options.label: B
options.text: Anterior compartment: Deep peroneal nerve; Lateral compartment: Superficial peroneal nerve; Posterior compartment: Tibial nerve

options.label: C
options.text: Anterior compartment: Tibial nerve; Lateral compartment: Deep peroneal nerve; Posterior compartment: Superficial peroneal nerve

options.label: D
options.text: Anterior compartment: Superficial peroneal nerve; Lateral compartment: Tibial nerve; Posterior compartment: Deep peroneal nerve

questions.answerText: Anterior compartment: Deep peroneal nerve; Lateral compartment: Superficial peroneal nerve; Posterior compartment: Tibial nerve
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Anterior compartment: Deep peroneal nerve; Lateral compartment: Superficial peroneal nerve; Posterior compartment: Tibial nerve

 

The leg has three compartments: anterior, lateral, and posterior, each with distinct functions, muscles, and nerve supply:

 

  1. Anterior Compartment:
    • Function: Dorsiflexion of the foot and extension of the toes.
    • Muscles: Tibialis anterior, extensor hallucis longus, extensor digitorum longus, and fibularis tertius.
    • Nerve Supply: Deep peroneal (fibular) nerve.
  2. Lateral Compartment:
    • Function: Eversion of the foot.
    • Muscles: Fibularis (peroneus) longus and fibularis brevis.
    • Nerve Supply: Superficial peroneal (fibular) nerve.
  3. Posterior Compartment:
    • Function: Plantarflexion of the foot and flexion of the toes.
    • Muscles: Gastrocnemius, soleus, plantaris, tibialis posterior, flexor hallucis longus, and flexor digitorum longus.
    • Nerve Supply: Tibial nerve.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The nerve supply of the compartments of the leg is as follows:

 

  • Anterior compartment: Deep peroneal nerve.
  • Lateral compartment: Superficial peroneal nerve.
  • Posterior compartment: Tibial nerve.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman presents with a complaint of unsteady gait. During examination, when asked to stand on her right leg, her left hip drops. This finding is not observed when she stands on her left leg. This clinical sign indicates weakness in which of the following muscles?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Right Gluteus Medius 

 

This scenario describes a positive Trendelenburg sign, which occurs when there is weakness or dysfunction of the gluteus medius and/or gluteus minimus muscles on the weight-bearing side. These muscles are responsible for stabilizing the pelvis during single-leg stance by preventing the opposite side of the pelvis from dropping.

 

Key points:

 

  1. Right Leg Weight-Bearing, Left Hip Drops:
    • Indicates weakness in the right gluteus medius and gluteus minimus, as they are unable to stabilize the pelvis when the patient stands on the right leg.
    • The superior gluteal nerve, which innervates the gluteus medius and minimus, may be affected.
  2. Normal Function:
    • The gluteus medius and minimus on the weight-bearing side contract to elevate and stabilize the opposite side of the pelvis.
  3. Clinical Presentation:
    • Opposite pelvis drop (OP): The pelvis drops on the side opposite to the weakened gluteus medius/minimus.
    • Ipsilateral lurch: Patients may lean their torso toward the weight-bearing side to compensate for the weakness.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Left Gluteus Medius: Incorrect. The left gluteus medius would stabilize the pelvis when standing on the left leg. The left side is unaffected in this case.

 

Option C. Right Gluteus Maximus: Incorrect. The gluteus maximus is responsible for hip extension and does not play a primary role in pelvic stabilization during single-leg stance.

 

Option D. Left Gluteus Maximus: Incorrect. The left gluteus maximus does not contribute to the stability of the pelvis during single-leg stance on the right leg.

 

Educational Objective:

 

A positive Trendelenburg sign indicates weakness of the gluteus medius and minimus on the weight-bearing side (in this case, the right side). These muscles are innervated by the superior gluteal nerve.

questions.stemHtml: A patient presented with painful vesicular eruptions as shown in image. Which division of trigeminal nerve is involved?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) V1

 

The image shows painful vesicular eruptions involving the forehead and upper eyelid region, consistent with Herpes Zoster Ophthalmicus. This condition occurs due to reactivation of the varicella-zoster virus (VZV) in the ophthalmic division (V1) of the trigeminal nerve (cranial nerve V).

 

Key features:

 

  1. Affected Area: The ophthalmic division (V1) supplies the skin of the forehead, scalp, upper eyelid, and the bridge of the nose. The vesicular eruptions follow the dermatomal distribution of V1.
  2. Hutchinson’s Sign: Vesicles on the tip of the nose indicate involvement of the nasociliary nerve, a branch of V1. This is often associated with ocular complications.
  3. Pain and Vesicles: The reactivation causes inflammation along the nerve distribution, leading to characteristic vesicles and severe pain.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. V2: Incorrect. The maxillary division (V2) supplies the midface, including the upper lip, cheeks, and lateral nose. Vesicles in this area are not observed in the image.

 

Option C. V3: Incorrect. The mandibular division (V3) supplies the lower face, including the lower lip, chin, and jawline. This region is unaffected in the image.

 

Option D. V4: Incorrect. There is no V4 division of the trigeminal nerve.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Herpes Zoster Ophthalmicus involves the ophthalmic division (V1) of the trigeminal nerve. Painful vesicular eruptions in the forehead and upper eyelid, particularly with Hutchinson’s sign, indicate V1 involvement.

questions.stem: Which chamber of the heart forms the base of the heart?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) LA and RA

 

The base of the heart is primarily formed by the left atrium (LA), with a minor contribution from the right atrium (RA). The base of the heart lies posteriorly and is in close relation to the esophagus and thoracic vertebrae.

 

Key details:

 

  1. The left atrium receives oxygenated blood from the pulmonary veins and contributes significantly to the base of the heart.
  2. The right atrium forms a smaller part of the base, receiving deoxygenated blood from the superior and inferior vena cavae.

 

The base is distinct from the apex of the heart, which is formed entirely by the left ventricle (LV).

 

Educational Objective:

 

The base of the heart is primarily formed by the left atrium (LA), with a minor contribution from the right atrium (RA). It is located posteriorly, opposite the apex.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old male patient presents with recurrent episodes of palpitations and dizziness. An echocardiogram reveals an enlarged right atrium and evidence of a right-to-left shunt. During the cardiac catheterization procedure, the cardiologist observes a valve-like structure within the right atrium. Which of the following structures guards the opening of the coronary sinus and may be contributing to the patient's symptoms?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Thebesian valve

 

The Thebesian valve is a small semicircular valve that guards the opening of the coronary sinus in the right atrium. Its role is to prevent the backflow of blood into the coronary sinus during atrial contraction. In certain conditions, the valve may become abnormally large or redundant, potentially interfering with proper cardiac blood flow and contributing to the patient’s symptoms.

 

Key points:

 

  1. Coronary Sinus: The coronary sinus drains deoxygenated blood from the heart's myocardium into the right atrium.
  2. Thebesian Valve: Guards the opening of the coronary sinus. An abnormal or thickened Thebesian valve may result in right atrial enlargement or impaired blood flow, as seen in this case.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Crista terminalis: Incorrect. The crista terminalis is a muscular ridge in the right atrium that separates the smooth posterior wall (sinus venarum) from the trabeculated anterior wall. It does not guard any valve or opening.

 

Option C. Mitral valve: Incorrect. The mitral valve is located between the left atrium and left ventricle, unrelated to the coronary sinus or right atrium.

 

Option D Eustachian valve: Incorrect. The Eustachian valve is a remnant of a fetal structure that guards the opening of the inferior vena cava (IVC) into the right atrium. It is unrelated to the coronary sinus.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The Thebesian valve guards the opening of the coronary sinus in the right atrium, while the Eustachian valve guards the opening of the inferior vena cava. Abnormalities of the Thebesian valve can lead to impaired venous drainage and right atrial enlargement.

questions.stemHtml: A 3-week-old male infant is brought to the pediatric clinic by his parents due to persistent respiratory distress and feeding difficulties since birth. The baby appears to have labored breathing, and the parents report that he frequently vomits after feeds. On physical examination, the infant is tachypneic with retractions and decreased breath sounds on the left side. A chest X-ray shows abdominal contents in the left thoracic cavity, confirming the diagnosis of a diaphragmatic hernia. Which of the following structure passes through the marked opening in the given image?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Vagus nerve

 

The marked opening in the image is the esophageal hiatus, located at the T10 vertebral level in the diaphragm. 

 

 

The following structures pass through the esophageal hiatus:

 

  1. Esophagus.
  2. Vagus nerves (both anterior and posterior branches).
  3. Left gastric vessels (small branches).

 

This opening is critical for allowing communication between the thoracic and abdominal cavities.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. IVC: Incorrect. The inferior vena cava (IVC) passes through the caval opening at the T8 level, along with the right phrenic nerve.

 

Option C. Aorta: Incorrect. The aorta passes through the aortic hiatus at the T12 level, along with the thoracic duct and azygos vein.

 

Option D. Greater splanchnic nerve: Incorrect. The greater splanchnic nerve passes through a small opening in the crura of the diaphragm, not the esophageal hiatus.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The esophageal hiatus (T10 level) allows the passage of the esophagus, vagus nerve, and left gastric vessels. This region is often implicated in conditions such as diaphragmatic hernias and gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD).




lux disease (GERD).

questions.stem: Portal vein is formed at which vertebral level
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) L2

 

The portal vein is formed by the union of the splenic vein and superior mesenteric vein (SMV) behind the neck of the pancreas at the L2 vertebral level. The portal vein then ascends to the liver, dividing into right and left branches within the liver.

 

Key points:

 

  • Splenic vein: Drains blood from the spleen and joins the SMV.
  • Superior mesenteric vein: Drains blood from the small intestine, cecum, and ascending colon.
  • Together, they form the portal vein, which is critical for transporting blood to the liver for detoxification and metabolism.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. T12: Incorrect. The T12 level corresponds to the aortic hiatus, where the aorta passes through the diaphragm, not the formation of the portal vein.

 

Option B. L1: Incorrect. L1 corresponds to the transpyloric plane, but the portal vein is formed slightly lower, at L2.

 

Option D. L3: Incorrect. The L3 level is lower than the actual site of the portal vein formation.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The portal vein is formed at the L2 vertebral level by the union of the splenic vein and the superior mesenteric vein behind the neck of the pancreas. This is a crucial anatomical landmark in abdominal circulation.

questions.stem: Fascia related to penis, scrotum & perineum are

options.label: A
options.text: Buck’s fascia, dorto’s fascia, colle’s fascia

options.label: B
options.text: Dorto’s fascia, colle’s fascia, buck’s fascia

options.label: C
options.text: Buck’s fascia, colle’s fascia, dorto’s fascia

options.label: D
options.text: Colle’s fascia, dorto’s fascia, buck’s fascia

questions.answerText: Buck’s fascia, dorto’s fascia, colle’s fascia
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Buck’s fascia, dorto’s fascia, colle’s fascia

 

The fascia related to the penis, scrotum, and perineum can be remembered using the mnemonic "BD Chaurasia" to recall their sequential arrangement:

 

  1. Buck’s fascia (B): Associated with the penis, this deep fascia encases the corpora cavernosa and corpus spongiosum.
  2. Dartos fascia (D): Found in the scrotum, this fascia contains smooth muscle fibers responsible for regulating scrotal skin temperature.
  3. Colle’s fascia (C): This is the superficial perineal fascia, located in the perineum. It is continuous with Scarpa's fascia from the abdomen.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The fasciae in the order from penis to scrotum to perineum are:

 

  • Buck’s fascia for the penis.
  • Dartos fascia for the scrotum.
  • Colle’s fascia for the perineum.

questions.stemHtml: Where in the body is the tissue shown in the image typically found?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Articular Cartilage

 

The image shows hyaline cartilage, which is characterized by:

 

  1. Chondrocytes: Present within lacunae (white spaces).
  2. No visible fibers: Unlike elastic or fibrocartilage, hyaline cartilage has a smooth matrix without obvious fibrous elements.
  3. Hyaluronic acid-rich matrix: This provides a glossy, homogenous appearance.

 

Hyaline cartilage is commonly found in:

 

  • Articular cartilage: Covers the ends of long bones within synovial joints.
  • Costal cartilage: Connects ribs to the sternum.
  • Growth plates: Found in developing bones (epiphyseal cartilage).
  • Respiratory cartilage: Found in the trachea, bronchi, and nasal septum.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Intervertebral disc: Incorrect. The intervertebral disc is composed of fibrocartilage, which contains thick collagen fibers visible in histology.

 

Option C. Eustachian tube: Incorrect. The Eustachian tube contains elastic cartilage, which shows elastic fibers not visible in the provided image.

 

Option D. Ear pinna: Incorrect. The ear pinna also contains elastic cartilage, not hyaline cartilage.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The tissue in the image is hyaline cartilage, commonly found in articular cartilage, growth plates, and the respiratory tract. It is characterized by chondrocytes in lacunae, a smooth extracellular matrix, and no visible fibers.

questions.stemHtml: Identify the histological slide given below
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Skin 

 

The histological image shows:

 

  1. Keratinized stratified squamous epithelium: The outermost layer of the epidermis, characteristic of skin.
  2. Hair follicles: These are seen embedded in the dermis, indicative of skin tissue.
  3. Sebaceous glands: Associated with hair follicles, responsible for secreting sebum.
  4. Dermis: Contains connective tissue, blood vessels, and sweat glands.

 

These features are consistent with a histological section of skin.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Cartilage: Incorrect. Cartilage lacks keratinized epithelium, hair follicles, and glands. It is composed of chondrocytes in lacunae within a matrix.

 

Option B. Collagen: Incorrect. Collagen is a structural protein found in connective tissues and does not include stratified squamous epithelium or hair follicles.

 

Option D. Lymph node: Incorrect. Lymph nodes are composed of lymphoid tissue, including follicles, germinal centers, and sinuses, none of which are visible here.

 

Educational Objective:

 

This histological slide represents skin, identified by its keratinized stratified squamous epithelium, hair follicles, sebaceous glands, and underlying connective tissue.

questions.stem: The reason for the long left recurrent laryngeal is due to the persistence of which arch artery?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) 6th

 

The recurrent laryngeal nerve is associated with the 6th pharyngeal arch during embryological development. Its long course on the left side is due to the persistence of the 6th arch artery, which contributes to the formation of the ductus arteriosus (and later the ligamentum arteriosum).

 

On the right side, the 6th arch artery disappears, and the right recurrent laryngeal nerve loops around the right subclavian artery (a derivative of the 4th arch). On the left side, the nerve loops around the aortic arch near the ligamentum arteriosum, resulting in its longer course.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. 4th: Incorrect. The 4th arch artery contributes to the formation of the aortic arch on the left and the right subclavian artery on the right but is not directly related to the recurrent laryngeal nerve.

 

Option B. 5th: Incorrect. The 5th arch either regresses or has no significant contribution in humans.

 

Option D. 7th: Incorrect. The 7th arch artery contributes to the formation of the distal portion of the subclavian artery but does not influence the recurrent laryngeal nerve.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The long course of the left recurrent laryngeal nerve is due to the persistence of the 6th arch artery, which forms the ductus arteriosus (ligamentum arteriosum postnatally).

questions.stem: Which of the following is correct sequence of functional column of cranial nerve nuclei from medial to lateral side

options.label: A
options.text: GSE→ SVA→ GVE → GVA→ SVE→ GSA→ SSA

options.label: B
options.text: GSE→ SVA→ GVA → GVE→ SVE→ GSA→ SSA

options.label: C
options.text: GSE→ SVA→ GVE → GSA→ SVE→ GVA→ SSA

options.label: D
options.text: GSE→ SVE→ GVE → GVA→ SVA→ GSA→ SSA

questions.answerText: GSE→ SVE→ GVE → GVA→ SVA→ GSA→ SSA
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) GSE→ SVE→ GVE → GVA→ SVA→ GSA→ SSA

 

The cranial nerve nuclei are arranged in specific functional columns along the brainstem, transitioning from efferent (motor) nuclei medially to afferent (sensory) nuclei laterally. The sulcus limitans serves as the dividing line between motor (efferent) and sensory (afferent) components.

 

 

 

Here is the correct sequence from medial to lateral:

 

  1. GSE (General Somatic Efferent): Supplies skeletal muscles derived from somites (e.g., extraocular muscles, tongue).
  2. SVA (Somatic Visceral Afferent): Supplies muscles derived from branchial arches (e.g., facial muscles, pharynx).
    GVE (General Visceral Efferent): Parasympathetic innervation to viscera.
  3. GVA (General Visceral Afferent): Sensory input from viscera.
  4. GSA (General Somatic Afferent): Sensory input from skin, muscles, and joints.
  5. SSA (Special Somatic Afferent): Special sensory input (e.g., vision, hearing, balance).

 

This functional arrangement reflects both development and the structure of the brainstem.

 

Mnemonic

 

To remember the sequence from medial to lateral:



"GSE → SVE → GVE → GVA → SVA → GSA → SSA."
 

  • GSE: General motor for somatic structures.
  • SVE: Motor for branchial arches.
  • GVE: Parasympathetic motor to viscera.
  • GVA: Sensory from viscera.
  • GSA: Sensory from skin and skeletal structures.
  • SSA: Special senses like vision and hearing.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The cranial nerve nuclei follow a medial-to-lateral organization based on function: GSE → SVE → GVE → GVA → SVA → GSA → SSA. Motor nuclei are medial, while sensory nuclei are lateral.

questions.stem: During embryonic development, the aortic arches play a crucial role in forming the major arteries of the head and neck region. The third aortic arch contributes to the formation of which important blood vessel?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Common carotid artery

 

The third aortic arch plays a crucial role in the development of the following major arteries:

 

  1. Proximal Part: Forms the common carotid artery (both right and left).
  2. Distal Part: Forms the proximal segment of the internal carotid artery.

 

The external carotid artery develops as a branch of the common carotid artery, and the vertebral artery is unrelated to the third aortic arch.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Internal carotid artery: Partially correct but not complete. The proximal segment of the internal carotid artery is derived from the third aortic arch. The rest of the internal carotid artery forms from the dorsal aorta.

 

Option C. External carotid artery: Incorrect. The external carotid artery arises as a sprouting branch from the common carotid artery, not directly from the third aortic arch.

 

Option D. Vertebral artery: Incorrect. The vertebral artery develops from the dorsal intersegmental arteries, not from any aortic arch.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The third aortic arch forms:

 

  • The common carotid artery (proximal part).
  • The proximal internal carotid artery (distal part).
    It does not directly contribute to the external carotid or vertebral arteries.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man presents to the urology clinic with complaints of painful urination and a sensation of burning at the tip of his penis for the past week. He mentions no history of similar symptoms in the past and denies any recent sexual activity. A physical examination reveals slight redness at the external urethral meatus. A urine sample is collected for analysis, and a swab is taken from the urethral tip for microscopic examination. Which type of epithelium is most likely to be found lining the tip of the urethra in this patient?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Non Keratinised stratified squamous epithelium

 

The epithelium lining the tip of the urethra (external urethral meatus) is:

 

  • Non-keratinised stratified squamous epithelium: This epithelium provides protection against mechanical friction and wet conditions, such as exposure to urine.

 

The urethra transitions through different epithelial types:

 

  1. Prostatic urethra: Lined by transitional epithelium.
  2. Membranous and spongy urethra: Lined by pseudostratified columnar epithelium.
  3. External urethral meatus (tip): Lined by non-keratinised stratified squamous epithelium.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The external urethral meatus is lined by non-keratinised stratified squamous epithelium, providing protection against mechanical friction and wet conditions.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man presents with a complaint of dragging his foot while walking. On examination, he demonstrates difficulty in dorsiflexing his foot at the ankle. This clinical presentation is most likely due to a lesion affecting which nerve?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Deep Peroneal (Fibular) Nerve

 

The clinical presentation of foot drop is characterized by the inability to dorsiflex the foot at the ankle. This condition is typically caused by injury or dysfunction of the deep peroneal nerve, which innervates the muscles responsible for dorsiflexion:

 

  1. Tibialis anterior: Main dorsiflexor of the foot.
  2. Extensor hallucis longus and extensor digitorum longus: Assist in dorsiflexion and toe extension.

 

The deep peroneal nerve is a branch of the common peroneal (fibular) nerve and runs in the anterior compartment of the leg. Lesions can occur due to trauma, compression, or neuropathy.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Sciatic Nerve: Incorrect. While the sciatic nerve branches into the common peroneal nerve and the tibial nerve, a lesion here would cause more extensive motor and sensory loss, not isolated foot drop.

 

Option C. Tibial Nerve: Incorrect. The tibial nerve innervates the posterior compartment of the leg, responsible for plantarflexion. A lesion here would impair plantarflexion, not dorsiflexion.

 

Option D. Sural Nerve: Incorrect. The sural nerve is a sensory nerve providing sensation to the posterior and lateral aspects of the leg and foot. It has no role in motor function or dorsiflexion.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Foot drop, characterized by the inability to dorsiflex the foot, is due to dysfunction of the deep peroneal nerve, which innervates the muscles of the anterior compartment of the leg.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a direct content of cavernous sinus?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Abducent nerve

 

The cavernous sinus is a dural venous sinus located on either side of the sella turcica. It has a unique arrangement of structures passing through it or along its walls.

 

Direct Contents of the Cavernous Sinus:

 

  1. Abducent nerve (CN VI): The only cranial nerve that runs through the sinus itself, close to the internal carotid artery.
  2. Internal carotid artery: Courses through the sinus, surrounded by the carotid plexus.

 

Structures in the Lateral Wall of the Cavernous Sinus:

 

  1. Oculomotor nerve (CN III)
  2. Trochlear nerve (CN IV)
  3. Ophthalmic branch (V1) of the trigeminal nerve
  4. Maxillary branch (V2) of the trigeminal nerve

 

These nerves lie in the lateral wall but do not directly course within the sinus cavity.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Oculomotor nerve: Incorrect. The oculomotor nerve runs in the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus, not within the sinus itself.

 

Option B. Trochlear nerve: Incorrect. The trochlear nerve also lies in the lateral wall, not as a direct content within the sinus cavity.

 

Option C. Maxillary branch of trigeminal: Incorrect. The maxillary branch of the trigeminal nerve (V2) runs in the lateral wall, outside the sinus.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The abducent nerve (CN VI) and internal carotid artery are the only direct contents of the cavernous sinus, while other cranial nerves lie in its lateral wall.

questions.stemHtml: A patient complains of headache with periorbital pain, tearing/ lacrimation, drooling of saliva, jaw spasm/pain, with light and accommodation reflex normal and pupils neither dilated nor constricted. Features of the patient can be explained by the involvement of which of the following?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) C

 

The patient’s symptoms, including periorbital pain, tearing, lacrimation, jaw spasm, and drooling of saliva, are hallmark features of trigeminal neuralgia. The trigeminal nerve (cranial nerve V) is primarily involved.

 

 

The trigeminal nerve has three divisions:

 

  1. Ophthalmic (V1) - Provides sensory innervation to the periorbital region.
  2. Maxillary (V2) - Responsible for sensory innervation to the midface, including the lacrimal gland and nasal structures.
  3. Mandibular (V3) - Provides sensory innervation to the lower face and motor innervation to the muscles of mastication, explaining the jaw spasm.

 

The lacrimation, tearing, and salivation are mediated through parasympathetic innervation associated with the trigeminal nerve via the pterygopalatine ganglion. Jaw spasm is due to involvement of the mandibular branch (V3), which innervates the muscles of mastication.

 

The light and accommodation reflexes being normal indicate that the third cranial nerve (oculomotor) is not affected, further pointing towards the trigeminal nerve as the culprit.

 

On the provided brainstem image, C corresponds to the trigeminal nerve, the largest cranial nerve originating from the ventral pons, confirming the answer.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. A (Olfactory Nerve): The olfactory nerve (cranial nerve I) is responsible for the sense of smell. It is unrelated to the described symptoms of periorbital pain, lacrimation, or jaw spasm.

 

Option B. B (Optic Nerve): The optic nerve (cranial nerve II) is responsible for vision and is not involved in the sensory or motor functions described in this patient’s case.

 

Option D. D (Facial Nerve): While the facial nerve (cranial nerve VII) plays a role in lacrimation and salivation, it does not explain the periorbital pain, conjunctival reflex involvement, or jaw spasm. These are specifically linked to the trigeminal nerve.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Trigeminal neuralgia involves the trigeminal nerve (cranial nerve V) and can cause periorbital pain, lacrimation, tearing, and jaw spasm due to its extensive sensory and motor functions. The nerve originates from the ventral surface of the pons, as seen in the labeled image (C).

questions.stemHtml: The cell marked in the below slide is inhibitory to:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Deep nuclei of cerebellum

 

The cell marked in the histological slide is a Purkinje cell, a large, distinctive neuron found in the cerebellar cortex.

 

  • Purkinje cells are the sole output neurons of the cerebellar cortex, and their axons project to the deep cerebellar nuclei, such as the dentate, interposed, and fastigial nuclei.
  • Purkinje cells release GABA (gamma-aminobutyric acid), an inhibitory neurotransmitter, which inhibits the activity of the deep cerebellar nuclei.
  • This inhibition plays a critical role in fine-tuning motor coordination and maintaining balance.

 

Thus, the Purkinje cell is inhibitory to the deep nuclei of the cerebellum, which process cerebellar output to other parts of the brain.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Vestibular nuclei: While the cerebellum sends information to the vestibular nuclei to assist in maintaining balance and posture, Purkinje cells do not directly inhibit the vestibular nuclei.

 

Option C. Inferior olivary nucleus: The inferior olivary nucleus provides climbing fibers to Purkinje cells, facilitating their activity. It is not inhibited by Purkinje cells.

 

Option D. Basal ganglia: The basal ganglia are involved in motor control and do not receive input from Purkinje cells.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Purkinje cells of the cerebellar cortex are inhibitory to the deep nuclei of the cerebellum, fine-tuning motor coordination and balance through GABAergic neurotransmission.
